# Platform Support Specification

Implemented public platform support, verification constraints, and platform-level lessons.

## Supported Platforms

| OS | Backend | Minimum |
|---|---|---|
| Windows | ConPTY (`CreatePseudoConsole`), or an out-of-band ConPTY the application supplies (`PtyStartInfo.ConPty`) | Windows 10 1809+, Windows 11 |
| Linux | `forkpty` + `execve` through native shim | Common glibc/musl targets |
| macOS | `posix_spawn` + `minipty_spawn_helper` through native shim | Supported runners; helper bundled in `runtimes/osx-*/native/` |
| FreeBSD (experimental) | `forkpty` + `execve` through native shim | `libutil`; built from source only |

**FreeBSD is experimental.** The backend is implemented and compiles when MiniPty is built on FreeBSD, but:

- It is tested neither locally nor in CI. Its termios, its hang-up behavior when the session leader exits, and its `kqueue` readiness follow from source only ([next_todo.md](../next_todo.md#unverified)).
- The package ships no FreeBSD binary. Through the package, `Pty.Start` fails because the shim cannot be loaded, so MiniPty works there only when built from source.
- One fork-child step Linux has is missing: inherited descriptors are not closed before exec (see the lessons below).

`Pty.IsSupported` still returns `true` on FreeBSD. It reports whether the operating system has pseudo-terminals MiniPty can drive, not whether this build ships a binary for it.

Pipe redirect without ConPTY is not a PTY. On Windows, TUI tools require ConPTY-backed spawn.

MiniPty does not use winpty or third-party PTY binaries. Backends are in-process interop plus the small Unix native shim. The out-of-band ConPTY (`conpty.dll` plus `OpenConsole.exe` from the `Microsoft.Windows.Console.ConPTY` package) is supplied by the application, never shipped by MiniPty; MiniPty is verified against package version `1.25.260930003`, pinned in `Directory.Packages.props` for its tests and Windows samples only ([Out-of-band ConPTY](core_session.md#out-of-band-conpty)).

## Verification

CI runs `tests/MiniPty.Tests` on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

| Check | Why |
|---|---|
| TTY detection (`redirected=False`, `isatty`) | Confirms real PTY semantics. |
| Simple command output | Confirms spawn and decode. |
| Stdin + EOF (`cat`, `sort`) | Confirms staged EOF. |
| Empty stdin EOF | Confirms staged EOF with no bytes: exit code 0, never `STATUS_CONTROL_C_EXIT`. |
| Multiple capture chunks + ANSI | Confirms concurrent read and timestamps. |
| `WaitForExitAsync` cancel vs `CompleteAsync` cancel | Confirms cancellation contract. |
| Resize | Confirms `TIOCSWINSZ` / `ResizePseudoConsole`. |
| Out-of-band ConPTY (Windows) | Confirms the loaded library's exports and host detection, which host process a session runs under (a Toolhelp census of this process's children), forwarding of the modes the in-box host consumes, no startup wait for the device attributes answer, and `Clear`. For both implementations: end of output on the pipe break once MiniPty has released its reference to the console server (in-box only where `kernel32.dll` exports `ReleasePseudoConsole`, probed by the test itself), the child's last output and a resize still arriving after the release. |

Tests use property assertions, not golden byte captures, to reduce OS and timing flake.

The PTY benchmarks come in two kinds that answer different questions, and their numbers must not be read across:

| Kind | Classes | Each operation | What the time says |
|---|---|---|---|
| Startup | `PtyStartupBenchmarks`, `PtyConPtyBenchmarks`, `PtyWebSocketBenchmarks` | spawns a child, reads its output, waits for its exit | spawn and exit cost, dominated by process creation (and on Windows by the console host); the allocations of each output path |
| Steady state | `PtyThroughputBenchmarks`, `PtyLatencyBenchmarks` | runs on one session started before the first operation | output throughput (`MiB/s` column) and keystroke round trip (per-keystroke percentiles) through the PTY, on MiniPty and on Porta.Pty |

Both use `MiniPty.Benchmarks.Child`, the same shell-free child on every OS; `dotnet build -c Release` copies it next to the benchmark assembly, and a missing child fails fast with a rebuild hint. The startup benchmarks' bulk scenarios run it as `--bytes <n>`, which writes *n* bytes in 4 KiB chunks and exits; `Echo` and `Exit0` still use lightweight shell commands where small spawn asymmetry is acceptable. The steady-state benchmarks run it as `--serve <n>`: it switches its input to raw (`stty raw -echo` on Unix, key events on Windows), then answers a trigger byte with *n* bytes of 77-character lines and an end marker, and any other byte with an echo into column 0. Markers and echoes alternate between two values, because ConPTY sends only what changed on its screen and may repaint what is already there.

On Windows the steady-state benchmarks run on both ConPTY implementations (`ConPty` parameter: `in-box`, and `out-of-band` when the package's files are staged); elsewhere the parameter is `none`.

Both steady-state classes also run Porta.Pty, the maintained .NET PTY library closest to MiniPty, on the same child. The harness gives it the same terminal size and marker scan, and a 16 KiB read buffer, the size of MiniPty's output ring. Each class has three methods:

- `MiniPty` is the baseline.
- `PortaPty` runs Porta.Pty as it starts by default: blocking pipes, so each `ReadAsync` holds a thread-pool thread.
- `PortaPtyAsyncIo` sets `UseAsyncIo`, so no thread is held while the session is idle.

Porta.Pty is referenced by the benchmark project only; MiniPty itself takes no dependency.

Steady-state measurements (2026-10-27, Ryzen 9 7950X3D; Windows 11 build 26200, Linux on WSL Ubuntu 24.04; three runs on Windows, ranges where runs differed):

| | Keystroke round trip (P50 / P95) | Throughput, 64 KiB / 1 MiB floods | Allocated per operation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Windows, in-box ConPTY | 7.3–7.4 / 7.7–8.0 ms | 8.8–9.0 / 8.9–9.0 MiB/s | 0 B |
| Windows, out-of-band ConPTY | 73–85 / 94–125 µs | 12.5–13.2 / 13.4–13.6 MiB/s | 0 B |
| Linux | 128–136 / 161–196 µs | 133–139 / 148–199 MiB/s | 0 B |

What sets each figure, from comparisons outside BenchmarkDotNet:

- **Windows: ConPTY.** The in-box host paints the echo on its own frame schedule, so a keystroke takes about 7.4 ms there and under 0.1 ms on the out-of-band host through the same MiniPty path. Floods run at the rate each host renders lines.
- **Linux throughput: the child and the kernel.** A C program that drives the same child with `forkpty` and blocking `read`/`write` on the master moved 64 KiB floods at 141 MiB/s; MiniPty, at 135–139 MiB/s, adds about 5%.
- **Linux keystrokes: thread wake-ups.** Back to back, the raw program's round trip was 52 µs (P50) and MiniPty's 70 µs (mean). With 10 ms of idle between keystrokes, as a typing user leaves, they were 116 µs and 185 µs: MiniPty wakes its I/O loop thread for the write and a thread-pool thread for the reader, which a blocking loop on one thread does not. BenchmarkDotNet's figure lies between the two, because its harness idles briefly between iterations.
- **Allocations: none.** A loop that awaits the round trips allocated 0.0 B per keystroke and per flood on Linux, idle gaps included.

Against Porta.Pty 2.2.3 (2026-10-28, same machine, three runs on each OS, ranges across runs). The MiniPty figures here are lower than in the table above: the machine was slower that day (see the lessons).

| | MiniPty | Porta.Pty | Porta.Pty, `UseAsyncIo` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Keystroke P50, Windows in-box | 7.29–7.43 ms | 7.61–7.68 ms | 7.59–7.66 ms |
| Keystroke P50, Windows out-of-band | 81–93 µs | 82–85 µs | 75–76 µs |
| Keystroke P50, Linux | 129–158 µs | 131–189 µs | 128–142 µs |
| 1 MiB flood, Windows in-box | 7.1–8.3 MiB/s | 7.3–8.8 MiB/s | 6.1–8.7 MiB/s |
| 1 MiB flood, Windows out-of-band | 11.7–12.7 MiB/s | 12.8–13.5 MiB/s | 13.1–13.4 MiB/s |
| 1 MiB flood, Linux | 157–186 MiB/s | 154–168 MiB/s | 180–184 MiB/s |
| Allocated per keystroke, Windows out-of-band / Linux | 0 B / 0 B | 376 B / 680 B | 248 B / 736 B |
| Allocated per 1 MiB flood, Windows out-of-band / Linux | 0 B / 0 B | 885 KB / 110–114 KB | 1,016 KB / 19–21 KB |

- **Speed is mostly even, but not on Windows out-of-band.** The terminal or the child sets the time, so most differences between the libraries fall within the spread between runs. On the in-box ConPTY, MiniPty's keystrokes were about 3% faster in every run.
- **On the out-of-band ConPTY, Porta.Pty was ahead in every run, until the Windows driver stopped posting reads into the ring.** Its floods were 5–10% faster, and with `UseAsyncIo` its keystrokes were about 8% faster. MiniPty's fastest flood iterations matched Porta.Pty's (about 74 ms per MiB), but more of its iterations were slow (80–100 ms). The cause was CPU per read, not waiting:
  - The out-of-band host sends a flood as about 4,100 writes of about 256 B per MiB.
  - On each write MiniPty's driver took three thread-pool hops: the zero-byte read's completion, the consumer's continuation, and the completion of a read posted into the ring and then canceled with `CancelIoEx`. The driver posted that ring read because the published chunk was still unread. It canceled it as soon as the consumer had read everything, which a consumer that keeps up does on every write.
  - Counted outside BenchmarkDotNet, a 1 MiB flood took about 12,000 thread-pool work items and 219–234 ms of CPU in MiniPty's process. Porta.Pty with `UseAsyncIo` took about 8,200 work items and 156–172 ms.
  - Wall time on an idle machine was about the same (73–76 ms against 73–74 ms). Under BenchmarkDotNet the extra CPU showed up as slower and more variable iterations.
  - Pipe size is not the cause: both libraries use 4 KiB pipes.
  - The driver now always waits with a zero-byte read ([core_session.md](core_session.md)). Counted the same way, in alternating runs against the previous build, a 1 MiB flood took about 8,180 work items and 141–172 ms of CPU (previously 12,000 and 219–234 ms), and a keystroke 2 work items instead of 3. Floods took 70.4–73.8 ms against 72.5–73.7 ms; keystrokes stayed within the spread between runs.

After that change (2026-10-28, three runs, ranges across runs):

| | MiniPty | Porta.Pty | Porta.Pty, `UseAsyncIo` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Keystroke P50, Windows in-box | 14.27–14.41 ms | 14.68–14.72 ms | 14.67–14.69 ms |
| Keystroke P50, Windows out-of-band | 73–81 µs | 70–82 µs | 71–78 µs |
| 64 KiB flood, Windows out-of-band | 13.4–14.0 MiB/s | 13.5–14.1 MiB/s | 11.9–13.7 MiB/s |
| 1 MiB flood, Windows in-box | 8.8–9.3 MiB/s | 8.9–9.2 MiB/s | 8.6–9.2 MiB/s |
| 1 MiB flood, Windows out-of-band | 13.2–14.2 MiB/s | 12.9–14.2 MiB/s | 12.8–14.0 MiB/s |

- On the out-of-band ConPTY, the libraries are now even: Porta.Pty's 1 MiB floods took 1.00–1.02 times MiniPty's time, and with `UseAsyncIo` 1.01–1.03 times. Allocations did not change: MiniPty allocated nothing.
- Every library's in-box keystroke took about twice as long as in the earlier runs that day (14.3–14.7 ms against 7.3–7.7 ms), so the in-box host's frame timing had changed, not the code (see the lessons). MiniPty's in-box keystrokes stayed 2–3% faster.
- **Porta.Pty allocates on every read.** On Windows out-of-band it wraps the output in a stream that hides ConPTY's startup query, and that stream implements only the `Task`-returning `ReadAsync`. On the in-box ConPTY it allocated 0–160 B per operation. MiniPty allocated nothing, apart from rare one-run fractions: 12 B per flood once, and 136 B per keystroke once on the in-box ConPTY. The size fits a thread-pool thread added during the run (see the lessons).

`PtyConPtyBenchmarks` runs the spawn, echo, and 32 KiB scenarios on the in-box and the out-of-band ConPTY side by side (`[Params] OutOfBand`); it reports 0 where `conpty.dll` is not staged, so it is Windows-only in effect. It is what showed that the out-of-band path ends output about 100 ms earlier per session, and that a caught exception on the disposal path cost each session 330 B ([lessons](core_session.md#lessons-learned)). Once the in-box ConPTY was released as well (Windows 11 24H2 and later), it showed both paths at the same times on build 26200: in-box `cmd /c echo` went from 150 ms to 37 ms and 32 KiB from 191 ms to 74–75 ms, and `PtyStartupBenchmarks` (then `PtyIntegrationBenchmarks`), which runs in-box on Windows, fell from 140–198 ms to 35–82 ms per scenario with no allocation added.

Allocation regressions are checked with `scripts/compare-benchmark-allocations.ps1` against
`BenchmarkDotNet.Artifacts/baselines/integration.json`; the gate is allocated bytes less than or
equal to the recorded baseline. Refresh that baseline only when an intentional lifecycle change
alters the measured path, and record the reason. The current one-shot baseline includes the bounded
post-exit quiet drain; persistent streaming and capture remain separate
benchmark categories because they use different orchestration.

## Platform-specific Test Constraints

These are verification choices, not API requirements, but they document pitfalls that broke CI when ignored.

| OS | Pitfall | Mitigation in tests |
|---|---|---|
| Linux | `bash -lc` on a PTY often stays interactive after `-c` completes. | Prefer `sh -c`, or spawn utilities directly. |
| Linux | A single EOT with no trailing newline does not signal EOF in canonical mode. | One-shot stdin tests using EOT end input with `\n` before `SendEof()`. |
| Windows | Ctrl+Z without a preceding line submit does not signal EOF for line-oriented readers. | `SendEof` submits a pending line with CR when input lacks a trailing `\r`/`\n`, then sends Ctrl+Z + CR; `PtyStdinEof_withoutTrailingNewline` covers Windows. |
| Linux | GNU `stty rows` / `stty columns` without arguments set size instead of printing it. | Query via `stty size`. |
| macOS | Spawn paths that do not attach a controlling terminal make `stty` and resize probes unreliable. | macOS uses `posix_spawn` + `minipty_spawn_helper` (controlling TTY via slave `open`); Linux/FreeBSD use `forkpty`. |
| macOS ARM | Variadic `ioctl` for `TIOCSWINSZ` is unsafe to P/Invoke directly. | Resize runs in `libminipty_unix`. |
| macOS | In canonical mode the tty keeps at most 1,024 bytes of a line (LF included) and, without blocking, drops later bytes, its LF and any EOT included, so a test child waits forever. Kill, interrupt, quit, and suspend free the line and lose the pending bytes. Erase and word erase free only what they remove. | Tests that need a write to wait, or EOF after a partial line, use short complete lines (`PtyInputTests`). |
| Windows | Closing ConPTY stdin yields `STATUS_CONTROL_C_EXIT`, also when no byte was ever written: a child about to exit on its own loses the race to the close under load (`PtyEmptyInputSignalsEof` on windows-2025 before the pipe close was dropped). | `SendEof` never closes the pipe; with no bytes written, it writes Ctrl+Z + CR on the first staging tick. |
| Windows | Input pipe close after bytes were written yields `STATUS_CONTROL_C_EXIT` for direct stdin readers (`sort`, `more`). | `SendEof` writes Ctrl+Z + CR and keeps the pipe open until exit; tests assert ExitCode 0 for `sort`. |
| Windows | `pwsh` is optional on runners. | Prefer built-in Windows PowerShell unless pwsh-only behavior is needed. |
| Windows (CI) | Tests that start the test executable as a descendants child time out on hosted runners when several start it at once, at the moment the parallel suite starts all its children (three at once on ARM64, one on windows-2025; 32 s for one under 3× CPU oversubscription on a desktop). | They share `[NotInParallel(DescendantsGroup)]`, so one such child starts at a time, and the pid-file wait is the 60 s `DescendantsStartTimeout` hang bound rather than the 30 s general one. |
| Windows (CI) | Once on windows-2025, a child copying console input (`find`) did not exit within 60 s of `SendEof` (`SendEofEndsInputWhoseLastByteIs0xFF`, started in the first second of the parallel suite). Not reproduced on a desktop: 20 runs of the test under 3× CPU oversubscription, 6 full suites pinned to four cores, and 960 such sessions started 32 or 64 at a time on four saturated cores all passed. | Tests that wait for exit after `SendEof` use `WaitForExitAfterEofAsync` (`PtyInputTests`), whose timeout reports where the child stopped: whether it had exited unreported, what it had copied, the console's last output (which echoes the `^Z` the host read), and whether a second EOF then ends it. |
| Linux (CI) | GitHub-hosted runners (including `ubuntu-24.04-arm`) may mount `/tmp` with `noexec`. Shebang execution of scripts under `/tmp` fails the start with `EACCES` even when `sh script` would work. | Integration tests that spawn executable fixtures use a directory under the test output (`AppContext.BaseDirectory`), not `Path.GetTempPath()`. PATH-overlay tests for plain scripts exercise the `ENOEXEC` → `sh` fallback, not shebang exec. |
| Linux (CI) | Tests that write a script and exec it at once can flake under parallel full-suite load (seen on `ubuntu-24.04-arm` in `PtyUnixPathLookupTreatsEmptyPathEntriesAsCurrentDirectory`). The likely cause is `ETXTBSY`: a child another test forks during the write holds the script's write descriptor until its own exec. That used to show as exit **127**; now it is `Win32Exception` 26 from `Pty.Start`. | `[Retry(3)]` on those tests; keep fixtures under `AppContext.BaseDirectory` (see row above). |
| Windows | A bare tool name can resolve to another program earlier on `PATH`: `find` started a Unix `find` that walked the file system instead of counting lines. | Tests start system tools by full path. |
| Windows | The console hands a line longer than the reader's buffer to the reader without waiting for CR, so the next Ctrl+Z starts a line and ends input whatever came before it. | Tests of the EOF chord after a partial line use a short partial line. |
| Windows | ConPTY's input pipe is also full while the console host is merely busy, so a write pending for an instant proves nothing about backpressure. | Tests that need ConPTY to have stopped reading input write until a write stays pending for 500 ms. |
| Windows (CI) | Hosted runners space ConPTY's output slices beyond the 500 µs coalescing window: 32 KiB arrived in 42–94 chunks against 13 on an idle desktop, and in 123, the uncoalesced count, on a desktop under 1.5× CPU oversubscription. No bound separates a slow host from a reader that does not coalesce. | Tests assert that every byte arrives and no chunk exceeds the output ring; the benchmarks track chunking. |
| Windows | Console hosts of other sessions start and end while a test runs, so "one more `OpenConsole.exe` child than before" is no evidence of which host a session runs under. | The census takes the set of child process ids before the start and waits for a new id to appear and later disappear. |
| Linux | A tty can take queued input after the child exits, so "end of output fails queued writes" holds only for writes still queued when output ends. | The deterministic test closes the transport while the child still runs. |
| Linux | A closed descriptor's number can be handed to the next one opened, so a before-and-after diff of open descriptors misses a leaked master under load. | Find a master by its terminal: `/proc/self/fdinfo/<fd>` reports `tty-index`, which matches the child's `/dev/pts/N`. |
| Unix | Closing the last reference to the master already hangs up the session leader, so a test of the explicit `SIGHUP` passes without it. | The child sets `CLOCAL` (on macOS the close then hangs nothing up), or the test holds a duplicate of the master (Linux). |
| Unix | A shell runs a trap only when its foreground command returns. | Children that trap `HUP` loop on `sleep 0.1` rather than block in `read` or a long `sleep`. |
| Windows | A program under a path of 260 characters or more starts only in a host that opted into long paths (`longPathAware` in its manifest), and only where the machine allows them (`LongPathsEnabled`); otherwise the opt-in is ignored. | The test host declares it in `tests/MiniPty.Tests/app.manifest`, which is the SDK's default manifest plus that one setting. `WindowsLongProgramPathTests` return early where the machine does not allow long paths, and one of them covers that case instead. |
| Windows | Benchmarks from a deep checkout fail to spawn: BenchmarkDotNet builds each job under `bin/Release/net10.0/<Job>/bin/Release/net10.0/`, which put the benchmark child at about 260 characters from a worktree under a temporary directory, and every benchmark that spawns it reported NA. | Run benchmarks from a short path. |
| Unix | `kill(pid, 0)` succeeds on a zombie. | "The pid is gone" also asserts that the exit watcher reaped the child. |
| macOS | When the 1 KiB output queue fills right after the CR of a newline, the terminal writes CR CR LF: it puts the CR again when it retries the LF. It happens only when the reader falls behind, at multiples of 1,024 bytes. | Tests that compare bulk output exactly fold `\r\r\n` into `\r\n` on macOS (`OneShotResultsKeepMultiMegabyteOutput`). |
| macOS | Output lost at the child's exit shows only when that exit is the terminal's last close. bash's exit was not, for a reason not identified, so it waited for the read even without MiniPty's own slave descriptor. | Tests of the child's last output use a zsh child, whose exit is the last close (`PtyMacExitDrainTests`). |
| macOS | A new terminal gets the lowest free number at once, so a test running alongside can open one under the name a session has just let go of, and the host then holds that name again. Each terminal gets a device node of its own, with a new inode, and the node goes once every descriptor of it is closed. The session leader's exit revokes the terminal, so a slave descriptor left open no longer shows under the name. | Tests that check a session let go of its terminal record the node's inode while the session runs and wait until the name no longer has it (`PtyMacExitDrainTests`). Asking `lsof` whether the host still held the name failed on macos-26-intel, and passed with the master and slave never closed. |
| macOS (CI) | A hosted Intel runner can be several times slower from one run to the next (the suite took 54 s, then 2 min 57 s). On the slow one a 1 MiB flood came at about 0.5 MB/s, below the rate at which the bridges join reads, so the bridges sent much of it read by read, as specified. | Frame-size tests check that their output came at least at the rate that starts a burst and are skipped below it; see [Terminal lessons](terminal.md#lessons-learned). |
| macOS | A master holds 1 KiB, so a child writing to it goes only as fast as the reader turns around. Discarding a hung-up child's output as it arrived took 1 MB in about 0.09 s on Apple silicon, and on the watcher's 10 ms polling alone about 82 KiB/s. The rate is shared, not per session: eight such children at once took about 0.5 s each, with the former reader threads as with the loop. | Hang-up discard tests write 256 KiB, about 40 ms discarded as it arrives and 3.2 s on polling alone, so the 1 s grace still tells the two apart, and they share `[NotInParallel(HungUpOutput)]`. With 1 MB both missed the grace together on macos-26-intel under the parallel suite, and in 3 of 3 full suites on an 8-core desktop with 16 busy loops beside it, where 256 KiB passed all 3. |

## Lessons Learned

- **Pipe redirect is not a PTY.** Redirected stdin/stdout captures bytes but children report not-a-TTY.
- **winpty is a poor fit for NativeAOT single-binary goals.** Bundled helpers add environment dependency; in-process ConPTY avoids that.
- **macOS spawn must establish a controlling terminal.** A bare `posix_openpt` + `posix_spawn` path left the slave without a controlling tty. macOS uses `posix_spawn` of `minipty_spawn_helper`, which `open`s the slave from `ttyname(STDIN)` before `execve`. Linux and FreeBSD keep `forkpty` + native `execve`.
- **macOS uses `posix_spawn` instead of `forkpty`.** Parallel CI and embedding hosts (.NET thread pool, many concurrent `Pty.Start`) hit burst PTY limits and fragile `fork` from a multithreaded parent. A global mutex around `forkpty` stabilizes CI but serializes every in-process spawn and was rejected; Darwin follows node-pty with `posix_spawn` + helper.
- **macOS `posix_openpt` can fail with a negative errno.** Under concurrent PTY open/close, far below `kern.tty.ptmx_max`, it fails with errno set to `-ENXIO` (-6). Mapping that to `EINVAL` made `Pty.Start` fail intermittently with errno 22 (about 3% of 25,600 spawns from 4 processes × 32 threads); the shim retries `posix_openpt` itself on a 1 ms interval and reports a persisting failure as `ENXIO`, which the spawn retry loop treats as transient. Mapping alone left about 0.04% of spawns failing under heavy parallel spawning, because re-running the whole spawn after its longer backoff exhausted every attempt.
- **macOS caps PTYs for the whole machine.** `kern.tty.ptmx_max` allows 511 by default (999 at most, and only root can raise it), and every terminal window and pane on the machine counts. A readiness probe opened 436 before `posix_openpt` failed with `ENXIO`. At the cap that error persists, so the spawn's retries for the transient case above only delay the failure. A macOS host cannot keep 1,000 sessions open without a raised limit ([readiness probe](../references/pty_crossplatform.md#readiness-on-a-pty-master)).
- **`minipty_fork_pty_exec` returns spawn errno.** Failures return a positive errno to managed code; do not rely on `SetLastError` across the native shim boundary.
- **Linux fork child scrubs inherited fds; FreeBSD fd scrub is follow-up.** After `forkpty`, Linux closes or marks close-on-exec on inherited descriptors `>= 3` and resets signal handlers to `SIG_DFL` before exec. FreeBSD gets signal reset only; inherited-fd close (`closefrom` or equivalent) remains open work — see [pty_crossplatform.md](../references/pty_crossplatform.md) → Fork child hygiene.
- **The exec payload need not outlive the spawn.** Holding it until disposal was believed to fix exit-127 flakes. A forked child reads its own copy-on-write image, so the parent's copy cannot affect it, which a measurement confirmed. The flakes most likely came from `ETXTBSY` on test fixtures written and executed at once. See [lifecycle.md](lifecycle.md).
- **Output must be read from spawn, not when a consumer gets scheduled.** Under burst parallel CI, `Task.Run` queued the blocking PTY read too late and fast macOS children closed the slave before output was captured (`PtyUnixParallelSpawnCompletes`); a macOS-only work-item scheduling fix and a rejected caller-side wait loop (thread-pool starvation, cancel-before-kill) preceded the current design. Every session now reads from spawn on every platform, through I/O completions on Windows and on the exit watcher's loop on Unix, with no consumer involved. See [pty_crossplatform.md](../references/pty_crossplatform.md) → Output pump.
- **Explicit Unix environments require `execve`.** Passing `envp` means MiniPty cannot rely on plain `execvp`; the native shim provides portable path lookup before `execve`.
- **Unix plain-script fallback differs from shebang exec.** `ENOEXEC` / `EACCES` / missing-interpreter `ENOENT` retry via `/bin/sh` then `/usr/bin/sh`. Shebang execution is attempted first and is sensitive to `noexec` mounts; see [pty_crossplatform.md](../references/pty_crossplatform.md) → Plain scripts and shell fallback.
- **Do not assume `/tmp` is exec-enabled on Linux CI.** Hardened runners treat `/tmp` as data-only; spawn tests that need executable fixtures belong under the build output tree or another exec-enabled path.
- **Capture timing requires concurrent reads.** Reading only after exit loses TUI animation timing.
- **A test's background process load belongs on dedicated threads, and it must reach the window it targets.** The Windows held-open-pipe test (`PtyWindowsOutputEndsWhileAnotherProcessHoldsTheOutputPipe`) first ran its spawners on `Task.Run`, and the blocked pool workers delayed the first session's `ReadOutputAsync` continuation by 11 s. The window the test targets is ConPTY's own `CreateProcess` of its console host, a few milliseconds per pseudo-console. A background load of 48 spawners, all started at once with a 3 s child each, ran in lockstep, in bursts of 48 children with nothing between them. During a 1.5 s loop of sessions it started nothing, and it hit the window in none of 12 sessions. The test now races `Process.Start` around `Pty.Start` on four dedicated threads and kills those children after each session. Those threads catch the `OperationCanceledException` that `ManualResetEventSlim.Wait(token)` throws on cancellation, because an exception that escapes a dedicated thread ends the test host. Its 2 s bound counts from the child's exit, not from `Pty.Start`: under 1.5× CPU oversubscription `cmd /c echo` alone took up to 3.2 s to exit, on a build from before the in-box release too, while output ended 0.2–0.6 s after exit. The ping children live about 10 s, so a held pipe still shows as seconds after a slow exit; with the forced end after the close removed, the test failed with output held about 10 s. The test kills them with `Process.Kill()`, not `Kill(entireProcessTree: true)`: a ping's only child is its console host, which exits with it, and the tree kill enumerates and opens every process on the machine on each call. Under the same oversubscription that took up to 8 s per ping, and one run spent 10 minutes killing pings while every MiniPty step of every session (start, end of output after exit, disposal) took under a second.
- **PTY output includes terminal echo.** Tests that drive stdin manually may capture echoed input and control characters.
- **Raw PTY text can break the parent console.** Use [Display text](display_text.md) helpers for logs or keep escaped/raw bytes for inspection.
- **Child-visible resize tests must synchronize with the parent.** Block the child until after parent `Resize` when asserting child-visible size.
- **Cross-OS integration benchmarks need the same bulk child on every OS.** OS-specific children (for example PowerShell `[string]::new` on Windows vs `head -c` on Unix) skew latency, bytes on the wire, and ConPTY read granularity, so CI compared harness noise instead of library cost. `MiniPty.Benchmarks.Child` isolates measurement; library-side ConPTY coalescing and drain polling are separate concerns documented in [core_session.md](core_session.md) and [pty_crossplatform.md](../references/pty_crossplatform.md).
- **A hang that does not reproduce gets a failure report, not a longer timeout.** The windows-2025 `SendEof` hang above passed every local reproduction, and nothing on MiniPty's side explains it: the input write and the Ctrl+Z + CR chord each fit the 4 KiB input pipe and complete synchronously, the exit watcher and the exit signal publish and read under full fences, and the byte 0xFF cannot hold back the bytes behind it, because the console host's UTF-8 input decoder (`til::u8u16`) maps lead bytes 0xF8–0xFF to length 0 and never caches them as a partial sequence. A longer bound would only hide the next occurrence, so the wait reports which stage stopped instead. A second EOF that ends the child means the first never reached it; output without the echoed `^Z` means the console host never read the chord.
- **Read the failure history before chasing one red run.** Three windows-2025 failures in a row named three different tests. Collecting every failed job's failing tests (`gh run list --status failure`, then each job's log) showed two of them already fixed (empty-stdin pipe close, descendants children starting together) and left one live case.
- **A benchmark that spawns per operation measures the spawn.** The startup benchmarks' times barely move with the path or the payload: on Linux every shell scenario took 11.0 ms and every 32 KiB scenario 41 ms, the difference being the .NET startup of the benchmark child, while 32 KiB crosses a PTY in well under a millisecond. Throughput and keystroke latency therefore run on one long-lived session, and the startup benchmarks are read for spawn cost and allocations only.
- **A benchmark child on a terminal must not use .NET's `Console` streams for raw I/O.** On Unix, `Console.OpenStandardInput`/`OpenStandardOutput` on a terminal initialize .NET's terminal handling: it writes terminfo strings, turns `isig` and `opost` back on after `stty raw -echo`, and reads input through its line reader. The first serve child echoed single keystrokes but never saw the throughput trigger, and the run hung. The child now reads and writes descriptors 0 and 1 through `FileStream`, and the harness fails an operation whose marker does not arrive within 60 s instead of waiting for the CI job's timeout.
- **A pooled async method awaited inside another one can allocate on every operation under BenchmarkDotNet.** The first steady-state runs showed 144 B per keystroke and about 135 B per flood on Linux, which looked like MiniPty's cost. The only type allocated was the state-machine box of the harness's own read method, nested in the benchmark's async method. BenchmarkDotNet waits for an operation on its own thread, while the nested method completed on a thread-pool thread and returned its box to that thread's cache, so the next operation on the benchmark thread rented a new box. Waiting the same way outside BenchmarkDotNet reproduced it (144 B per keystroke on the waiting thread), and awaiting the same round trips allocated nothing. The harness now makes each operation one pooled async method that the benchmark returns as its result, and every steady-state figure reads 0 B.
- **ConPTY sends only the cells that changed, so whatever a benchmark waits for must change every cell it looks at.** A flood that ConPTY takes in within one frame leaves a screen that differs from the one two operations earlier only in the end-marker row. With markers that differed in one letter, ConPTY sent that letter alone, and the harness never saw a whole marker. The two markers now differ in every position, and a keystroke's echo overwrites column 0 with a byte that alternates.
- **The in-box ConPTY at times withholds output it has rendered until its screen changes again.** About once in 5 to 10 runs of `PtyThroughputBenchmarks`, a flood's end never arrived. The child's own log showed the flood written; at the stall MiniPty had a zero-byte read posted on the output pipe, nothing unread, and `PeekNamedPipe` showed nothing in the pipe, so ConPTY had sent nothing. Another keystroke made the whole flood arrive at once. In 15 runs on the out-of-band ConPTY it never happened. The harness nudges an overdue flood with a keystroke after 5 s and reports it on the console; the nudged iteration is an outlier the summary drops. A terminal frontend on the in-box ConPTY can meet the same thing as output that appears only with the next keystroke.
- **Latency percentiles need one operation per iteration and every outlier kept.** BenchmarkDotNet averages the invocations of an iteration and drops upper outliers by default, which would remove the slow keystrokes a user notices. `PtyLatencyBenchmarks` runs with invocation count 1 and `OutlierMode.DontRemove`; its warning that the iteration time is small does not apply to a measurement of a single round trip.
- **A comparison library must run on the ConPTY its label says.** Porta.Pty looks for `conpty.dll` only beside its assembly and for the host at `<that directory>\<arch>\OpenConsole.exe`, and otherwise falls back to the in-box ConPTY without an error. A portable build keeps both under `runtimes\win-<arch>\native\`, where MiniPty finds them and Porta.Pty does not. The benchmark build therefore copies this architecture's two files to the output root and the host to `<arch>\` as well, so both libraries load the same files. A Porta.Pty case fails unless `PtyProvider.PseudoConsoleImplementation` reports the ConPTY it measures, and every out-of-band case fails unless an `OpenConsole.exe` from the benchmark output is running. The first run stopped on the first check: Porta.Pty reported `oob-no-host`.
- **Porta.Pty on Windows passes exactly the environment it is given.** An empty `Environment` dictionary starts the child with no environment at all. The harness passes the whole current environment, as MiniPty inherits it by default.
- **Compare libraries only within one run.** On 2026-10-28 the same MiniPty build took 89 ms per 1 MiB out-of-band flood, against 73–74 ms the day before. The harness in HEAD and the new one gave the same figure in alternating runs, so the machine had changed, not the code. Machine state moved absolute figures by 20%, more than the difference between the libraries. Later the same day the in-box ConPTY's keystroke round trip doubled for all three libraries at once (7.3–7.7 ms to 14.3–14.7 ms), the host's frame timing again, while the out-of-band figures held.
- **Benchmark persistent, one-shot, and capture paths separately.** They intentionally differ in pump ownership, buffering, materialization, and drain behavior; collapsing them into one number hides regressions and can reward an implementation that violates another path's contract.
- **Read an allocation figure for what it counts.** Measure a baseline in the same checkout path as the change: spawn allocations grow with the executable and working-directory path lengths, and a baseline taken under a long worktree path came out about 1.5 KB higher. BenchmarkDotNet refuses to build while another copy of the benchmark project sits under the repository, as a worktree does. Async paths jitter by roughly 50–400 B between runs and a single run occasionally doubles, so compare several runs before attributing a delta. On Linux the streaming benchmarks' child was still unreaped at disposal in 296–300 of 300 iterations, because output ends on `EIO` before the exit watcher reaps, so every per-disposal cost of the running-child path lands in their figures.
- **A fraction of a byte per operation is usually a wait, not a leak.** BenchmarkDotNet's allocation column counts every thread, so a thread-pool thread added mid-run (about 1 KB) shows as a fraction of a byte per operation. It also waits on a pending `ValueTask` through `UnsafeOnCompleted` with an `Action`, which queues an allocated work item, 32 B, for each write that had to wait; `await` allocates nothing there. The input benchmark writes faster than the terminal reads, so about one write in 64 waits on Windows (the 4 KiB pipe buffer) and one in 16 on macOS (about 1 KiB of tty), which reads as 2 B/op on macOS and about 0.5 B/op on Windows, rounded half to even to 0 B or 1 B.
- **A test can pass for the wrong reason, so confirm it red against a mutation of the code it covers.** Tests that passed without their fix: a kill-on-cancellation test that waited 30 s for a child that exits by itself after about 30 s; an EOF-ordering test that drained output before the first staging tick, so EOF never waited for the queue, and whose line count could not see reordered parts; a 0xFF test that compared only the byte before 0xFF; a queued-input test whose echo woke the reader and hid a missing wake, until its child turned echo off and the test waited for a marker printed after that; a thread-pool test whose cap was below the minimum, so `SetMaxThreads` returned false and changed nothing; a drive-relative `C:` `PATH` entry that never reached the planted file (`Path.Join("C:", name)` is `C:\name`), where `C:empty\..` does; and a macOS check that the host no longer held the terminal's name after disposal, which passed with the master and slave never closed, because the session leader's exit had revoked the terminal and only the master kept its node. Apply and revert a mutation by line or by a string that occurs once: a revert by pattern also changed two other lines that no filtered test exercised.
- **A consistent CI failure is a deterministic failure in that environment, not a flake.** Hosted runners have 3–4 cores and run the suite beside dozens of PTY children, so a thread sleeping 50 ms is routinely scheduled 100 ms later. Each hosted failure after the GUI-host work was reproduced or explained on a desktop before it was fixed, mostly by running the same tests under CPU oversubscription, which also separated a timing margin from the full-ring defect it had hidden.
- **Bound every background load in a measurement.** A probe that started processes in an unbounded loop accumulated about 16,000 console processes within minutes, because each console child also starts a console host and process creation slows as they pile up. Cap concurrency and wait for each child.
- **Process exit can only be tested from outside the process.** An in-process test that calls the exit handler stays green when the subscription is deleted. The test executable serves as the host: a module initializer runs the host code and exits before the test framework starts. That code stays synchronous on the initializing thread, because code from the same assembly on another thread waits for the module initializer to finish.
- **A disposed `ManualResetEventSlim` throws from `Wait` even when it is set.** A test that disposed an event its queued work could still wait on ended the test process from a pool thread in 2 of 6 to 5 of 20 full runs.
